subject: Civil Engineering
title: How Earthquakes Happen
description: A fast breakdown of How Earthquakes Happen for builders.

hook.text: The ground beneath your feet is moving right now — inches per year, building stress.

buildup.text: Tectonic plates float on molten rock. Where they collide, stress builds along faults.

discovery.text: When the stress exceeds friction, the fault ruptures. Stored energy releases as seismic waves.

twist.text: The rupture can last seconds — but the shaking travels hundreds of miles in every direction.

climax.text: The San Andreas Fault stores enough stress for a magnitude 8 — the next Big One is inevitable.

punchline.text: The Earth is always moving. Earthquakes are just when it lets go.

quiz.question: What causes an earthquake?
options: Underground volcanic explosions that shake the surface
Accumulated stress along a fault exceeds friction, causing sudden rupture
Heavy rainfall saturating the ground and triggering vibrations

details.summary: Earthquakes occur when accumulated stress in the Earth's crust exceeds the strength of rock along a fault, causing sudden rupture and slip. The released energy radiates outward as seismic waves from the focus, with the epicenter being the point on the surface directly above.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding earthquake mechanics is the foundation of earthquake engineering. The characteristics of fault rupture determine the ground shaking that structures must survive.
takeaways: Tectonic stress accumulates gradually until fault rock strength is exceeded
Energy radiates as seismic waves from the fault rupture zone
Most destructive earthquakes occur at plate boundaries or active faults

faq.question: Can earthquakes occur away from tectonic plate boundaries?
faq.answer: Yes. Intraplate earthquakes occur within plates along ancient buried faults. The 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes in central United States were among the largest in North American history.

faq.question: What determines how strong an earthquake's ground shaking will be at a particular location?
faq.answer: Ground shaking depends on earthquake magnitude, distance from the fault, depth of rupture, local soil conditions, and the direction of fault rupture propagation. Soft soil amplifies shaking compared to rock. Near-fault locations experience stronger shaking.
